_spec.purpose: A standalone web edition of the archived visual story.
_spec.law: Facts resolve to the original verified claim record. A layout rebuild does not reverify reporting.

dek.text: An AI tool flagged a gene for one Texas child with no diagnosis. Families found through a network and fruit fly experiments made it a likely diagnosis, not a certain one.

introduction.text: [The work began with a child enrolled in the Texome Project. The program provides free genetic testing for medically underserved people with rare and undiagnosed conditions](c5). [Standard genetic analyses of the child and a parent did not reveal an answer](c7). [Then a new AI tool called AI-MARRVEL analyzed the genomic data and highlighted a rare change in the BRSK1 gene as a promising candidate for a diagnosis](c8).

[Texas Children's Hospital put out its release on {{date:c1}}](c1). [It says researchers there and at Baylor College of Medicine and the Texome Project have identified BRSK1 variants as a likely diagnosis for a rare neurodevelopmental disorder](c3). [The study appears in the American Journal of Human Genetics](c4). The flag came from software. The case for it came from more families and from flies.

paragraphs.text: [AI-MARRVEL is described in a peer-reviewed paper in NEJM AI](c32). [It uses a random forest classifier trained on over {{number:c33}} million variants from thousands of diagnosed cases](c33). [Its developers report that it doubled the number of solved cases against the methods it was benchmarked with. The comparison covered three real world cohorts](c34).

[On one confidence metric it reached {{number:c35}} percent precision and found {{number:c35:1}} percent of the diagnosable cases in a collection of {{number:c35:2}}](c35). Precision and the share of cases found measure different things. Neither is an accuracy figure for this child. The tool's output was a candidate rather than a diagnosis.

sections.heading: What the families and the flies added

paragraphs.text: [The researchers shared the finding through a research network called GeneMatcher. Other families then reported rare variants in the same gene](c9). [GeneMatcher is a tool built to connect people interested in the same gene](c37). [The study grew to {{number:c10}} affected people from seven unrelated families](c10). [Every one of them showed some degree of developmental delay. The severity varied](c11). [Common features included delayed speech and language, intellectual disability, autism, ADHD, anxiety, low muscle tone and microcephaly](c12). [Two of them had seizures](c13).

[In fruit flies the gene's equivalent is called sff, for sugar-free frosting. It is active mainly in neurons](c16). [With the fly gene disabled the flies had trouble moving. They were more prone to seizure-like behavior and lived shorter lives](c17). [The normal human gene largely corrected those problems](c18). [The team modeled three of the patients' variants in flies](c29). [Each of the three gave only a partial rescue](c51), [which suggests the variants reduce the protein's activity without removing it](c19).

[Texome takes as candidates people from underserved populations with a suspected rare disease who can't pay for DNA sequencing](c39). [Its genetic testing and follow-up consultations come at no cost](c40). [The study runs {{number:c43}} visits over {{number:c43:1}} years in person or virtually](c43). [It re-evaluates key genes at six months, one year and two years](c50). [The project asks anyone who thinks they may be eligible to write to texome-project@bcm.edu](c42).

[The paper's authors conclude that losing one working copy of BRSK1 leads to a neurodevelopmental syndrome whose features vary](c31). The release calls the variants a likely diagnosis. This edition does not upgrade that to a certain one. [Texome states a plan to sequence about {{number:c46}} children with undiagnosed disorders](c46). The sources checked for this edition do not say how many it has reached.
